input: This work investigates the conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen to dimethyl ether over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst, focusing in particular on the influence of catalyst form, which is widely recognised to be an important factor in reactor performance. Two forms of the catalyst were compared using one feed composition: a structured catalyst and a pellet catalyst. Performance was measured in terms of the space-time yield, defined as the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). The tests were conducted at 250 °C and 50 bar, with a hydrogen-to-carbon-dioxide feed ratio of 3. The structured catalyst delivered a space-time yield of 0.9 kg L-1 h-1 with a pressure drop of just 0.23 bar, and it lost 7% of its activity after 100 h. The pellet catalyst, in contrast, delivered a space-time yield of 0.35 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 1.34 bar, and it lost 14% of its activity after 100 h. These findings clearly demonstrate the superiority of the structured form in terms of yield, pressure drop, and activity retention alike. It should nevertheless be borne in mind that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which makes paired comparisons of this kind especially valuable. Further work will of course be needed in order to establish how both forms behave over longer periods and under the wider range of conditions that industrial operation would inevitably involve in practice.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen are converted over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to dimethyl ether, and the catalyst form sets both the yield of a reactor and the pressure drop it imposes. Two forms were compared on one feed composition: a structured catalyst and a pellet catalyst. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Tests ran at 250 °C and 50 bar with a hydrogen-to-carbon-dioxide feed ratio of 3. The structured catalyst gave the higher space-time yield (0.9 kg L-1 h-1) at the lower pressure drop (0.23 bar), and lost 7% of its activity after 100 h. The pellet catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.35 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 1.34 bar, and lost 14% of its activity after 100 h. The structured form leads on all three reported measures at the tested conditions: the higher yield is a smaller catalyst volume for the same duty, the lower pressure drop is a lower compression duty on the feed, and the slower activity loss means the advantage at the start of a run is not surrendered later in the run. The activity loss figures are end-of-test values, and the two forms are compared at equal time on stream, so the retention advantage is a measured difference between the forms and not an extrapolation from unlike runs. The comparison is bounded: no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so sulfur tolerance is unknown for both forms, and yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, so the paired data reported here carry the preference.
